article_title: Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning
citation: Manuela Macedonia, Lihui Hu, Brian Mathias. (2026). Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10222-8
title: Gesture Memory Support Model (GMSM): seven dimensions for characterizing instructional gestures
description: The GMSM is a preliminary theoretical and operational framework for characterizing instructional gestures in L2 vocabulary learning. As the article states, it is "a preliminary theoretical and operational framework, accompanied by provisional rating guidance, for characterizing instructional gestures according to seven dimensions hypothesized to be relevant to their potential mnemonic contribution to L2 vocabulary learning". The dimensions capture properties of the gesture stimulus and its relationships with the target word, learners, and context, and are retained as a multidimensional profile rather than combined into one effectiveness score. The dimensions are not assumed to be statistically independent or additive.
requirements: Rating guidance for characterizing gestures dimension by dimension; dimensions rated in relation to the intended lexical meaning rather than gesture category membership
constraints: Not an empirically validated diagnostic or predictive instrument; reliability and empirical distinctiveness of dimensions remain to be established; grounded primarily in L2 research; facial expression considered only for emotional salience fit, with prosody, gaze, and posture outside the core dimensions
examples: The article contrasts the GMSM's multidimensional profile approach with traditional taxonomies such as McNeill's Quartet and Kendon's Continuum, which classify spontaneous co-speech gestures rather than designed instructional gestures
key_sources: Manuela Macedonia, Lihui Hu, Brian Mathias. (2026). Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10222-8

article_title: Effectiveness of a Parent-Child Home Numeracy Intervention on Urban Catholic School First Grade Students
citation: Lore, M. D., Wang, A. H., & Buckley, M. (2016). Effectiveness of a Parent-Child Home Numeracy Intervention on Urban Catholic School First Grade Students. Journal of Catholic Education, 19(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.15365/joce.1903082016
title: GMADE Level 1 standardized mathematics assessment as outcome measure
description: The Group Mathematics Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation (GMADE) Level 1, Forms A and B, a norm-referenced test, served as the outcome measure. "Student mathematics performance was measured at preintervention and postintervention using the standard scores" of the GMADE, with subtests Concepts and Communication, Operations and Computation, and Process and Applications combined into a Total Score. Form A was used at pretest and Form B at posttest to control for recall; the same trained researcher administered the test at both sites.
requirements: Forms A and B alternated between pretest and posttest to control for recall
Same trained administrator at both sites for reliability
constraints: Subtest scores were multicollinear (correlations .81 to .91 at posttest), so only Total Test scores were used for group comparisons
target_learning_goals: Standardized mathematics achievement across number and operations, algebra, geometry, measurement, and data analysis
examples: The article reports the GMADE was strongly predictive of TerraNova (r = .85) and ITBS (r = .90) scores
key_sources: Lore, M. D., Wang, A. H., & Buckley, M. (2016). Effectiveness of a Parent-Child Home Numeracy Intervention on Urban Catholic School First Grade Students. Journal of Catholic Education, 19(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.15365/joce.1903082016

article_title: Association between resident physicians from foreign medical schools and general medicine in-training examination scores: a nationwide cross-sectional study in Japan.
citation: Ishizuka Kosuke, Nishizaki Yuji, Sekine Miwa, Shimizu Taro, Shikino Kiyoshi, Yamamoto Yu, Fukui Sho, Nojima Masanori, Ohta Mitsuyasu, Tokuda Yasuharu. (2026). Association between resident physicians from foreign medical schools and general medicine in-training examination scores: a nationwide cross-sectional study in Japan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08941-1
title: General Medicine In-Training Examination (GM-ITE®) as a nationwide standardized knowledge assessment for Japanese residents
description: The GM-ITE is a nationwide standardized assessment aligned with Japan's clinical training guidelines, administered at the end of PGY-1 and PGY-2 to evaluate resident physicians' test-based clinical knowledge. The 2023 version comprised 80 multiple-choice questions across four categories and six clinical fields, with 10 questions in English. It "does not aim to establish equivalence or superiority across groups, but rather provides a common assessment framework within which exploratory comparisons can be descriptively examined" and serves not as a pass-fail examination but to identify proficiency and weaknesses.
requirements: A Japanese medical license, obtained by passing the Japanese National Medical Practitioners Qualifying Examination, is required before IMG residents undergo clinical training and take the GM-ITE.
constraints: It does not directly assess workplace-based competencies such as bedside performance, communication, teamwork, or procedural skills.
target_learners: Postgraduate year 1 and 2 resident physicians in Japan, including international medical graduates
target_learning_goals: Test-based clinical knowledge across Medical Interview and Professionalism, Symptomatology and Clinical Reasoning, Physical Examination and Clinical Skills, and Disease-Specific Topics categories and six clinical fields
examples: In 2024, 9,106 resident physicians from 669 institutions participated, with 6,366 consenting to this study (response rate: 69.9%).
key_sources: Ishizuka Kosuke, Nishizaki Yuji, Sekine Miwa, Shimizu Taro, Shikino Kiyoshi, Yamamoto Yu, Fukui Sho, Nojima Masanori, Ohta Mitsuyasu, Tokuda Yasuharu. (2026). Association between resident physicians from foreign medical schools and general medicine in-training examination scores: a nationwide cross-sectional study in Japan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08941-1

article_title: Resident Physician Recognition of Tachypnea in Clinical Simulation Videos in Japan: Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Shikino K, Nishizaki Y, Fukui S, Kataoka K, Yokokawa D, Shimizu T, Yamamoto Y, Nagasaki K, Kobayashi H, Tokuda Y. (2025). Resident Physician Recognition of Tachypnea in Clinical Simulation Videos in Japan: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72640
title: Clinical simulation video embedded in the GM-ITE assessing non-verbal cue recognition
description: A 5-minute video filmed from a resident physician's perspective showing a medical interview and physical examination of a 40-year-old man presenting with fainting after lower limb fracture, in whom the correct diagnosis was acute pulmonary thromboembolism. Tachypnea of "28 breaths per minute" was "not highlighted in the text, but presented as non-verbal cues," requiring observation without textual focus. Participants answered a free-text diagnosis question and listed three pertinent positive findings, with interrater agreement of κ=0.91 (Q1) and κ=0.82 (Q2). Produced by a professional television production company under JAMEP supervisors with professional actors and added heart-sound effects.
requirements: Participants must observe the video and answer open-ended diagnostic questions scored by trained raters
constraints: The video was a new GM-ITE addition, and the authors note the novelty of the format might have influenced participants' performance
target_learners: first- and second-year resident physicians in Japan
target_learning_goals: recognition of non-verbal clinical cues such as tachypnea
integration of verbal and non-verbal clinical information
examples: The video depicted tachypnea, jugular venous distension, and a right lower limb fracture, with actual heart sounds presented during auscultation
key_sources: Shikino K, Nishizaki Y, Fukui S, Kataoka K, Yokokawa D, Shimizu T, Yamamoto Y, Nagasaki K, Kobayashi H, Tokuda Y. (2025). Resident Physician Recognition of Tachypnea in Clinical Simulation Videos in Japan: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72640

article_title: Graduate medical education success coaching for residents and fellows: a single-institution real-world experience.
citation: Redman Charles, Chung Catherine G., McFarlane Daniel, Meara Alexa, Ejaz Aslam. (2024). Graduate medical education success coaching for residents and fellows: a single-institution real-world experience. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2342102
title: GME success coaching program for residents and fellows
description: A formal coaching program established in 2020 at Ohio State University, an institution with 80 ACGME-accredited training programs, in which three coaches selected from various training programs meet referred residents and fellows for needs assessment and periodic longitudinal coaching. The article describes it as "a learner-driven process with an emphasis on mindset and growth" in which coaches help learners "identify areas for improvement, specific goals, and strategies to achieve them." Strategies included personal coaching, professional coaching by certified non-GME coaches, emotional intelligence training, self-reflection, career counseling, simulation-lab clinical skills practice, employee assistance program referral, and focused feedback.
requirements: Coaches with prior experience in education and coaching who receive additional direct coaching training with an emphasis on professionalism
Referral either self- or program director-initiated, with services available to any referred resident or fellow without minimum requirements
Periodic meetings with both the program director and the learner to monitor longitudinal coaching goals
constraints: Coaching was voluntary and learners engaged until they achieved competency or graduation (range 4–30 months)
Meeting intervals were individualized and averaged 5.5 meetings per learner (range 2–25)
target_learners: Residents and fellows in graduate medical education
examples: Over three years the program served 29 referrals encompassing 21 different medical and surgical specialties
key_sources: Redman Charles, Chung Catherine G., McFarlane Daniel, Meara Alexa, Ejaz Aslam. (2024). Graduate medical education success coaching for residents and fellows: a single-institution real-world experience. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2342102

article_title: The practial use of the consensus statement on practical skills in medical school--a validation study.
citation: Blaum Wolf E., Dannenberg Katja A., Friedrich Torsten, Jarczewski Anne, Reinsch Anne-Katrin, Ahlers Olaf. (2012). The practial use of the consensus statement on practical skills in medical school – a validation study. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 29(4), Doc58. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2012-29/zma000828.shtml
title: GMA consensus statement "Practical Skills in Medical School" as a reference frame of 290 learning objectives
description: The consensus statement, developed by the GMA within the National Competency-Based Learning Objective Catalogue for Medicine (NKLM), is a reference frame for practical skills teaching. The article states it "describes 289 learning objectives, 232 of which are defined as core objectives", each assigned to at least one of 16 organ systems, with objectives divided by type (core or elective), stage of medical education, and level of instruction (demonstration, supervised performance, skilled performance). In this study it served as the mapping reference against which the tutorial program was classified.
requirements: Learning objectives must be assignable to organ systems, objective type, stage of medical education, and a defined level of instruction for mapping to work
constraints: The study found ambiguous formulation and unspecific scope of some objectives left room for interpretation during classification
examples: Four evaluators classified all 290 objectives across 48 tutorials (13,920 classifications) to map the Charité Learning Center's peer-teaching program.
key_sources: Blaum Wolf E., Dannenberg Katja A., Friedrich Torsten, Jarczewski Anne, Reinsch Anne-Katrin, Ahlers Olaf. (2012). The practial use of the consensus statement on practical skills in medical school – a validation study. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 29(4), Doc58. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2012-29/zma000828.shtml
